To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mixture of alignments, computed from the second-or even higher- order scatter tensors, of the features extracted by two CNN streams trained with the proposed So-HoT loss, is a very powerful tool for domain adaptation.

(i) second-or higher-order statistics can be used to improve the performance in domain adaptation; and (ii) the proposed method is effective in the supervised target setting where only a few labeled target samples are available.

(a) Second-order scatter statistics are a useful tool for domain adaptation, (b) Second-order scatter tensors are more discriminative than first-order ones, (c) Second-order scatter alignment improves domain adaptation, (d) Higher-order scatters are even more discriminative, and (e) The proposed So-HoT approach is competitive with the state of the art on standard benchmarks
In summary, our research is concerned with
the supervised target scenario and we propose an approach for domain adaptation based on a mixture of alignments of scatter tensors.
the following questions. Can we learn to transfer knowledge from a source to a target domain with few target labeled training samples
the supervised domain adaptation problem, where few labeled samples per category are available in the target domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our So-HoT approach outperforms all other domain adaptation methods, including those based on the first-order scatter statistics, by a large margin.
So-HoT is the first method to achieve a state-of-the-art performance in the domain adaptation literature for both visual and depth-to-rgb domain adaptation tasks.
our approach outperforms the current state-of-the art on all datasets and scenarios.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed method is simple and effective, and can be easily extended to higher-order statistics.
we show how to transfer knowledge between domains in a way that is both efficient and accurate.
we have shown how second-or even higher- order scatter tensors can be used for domain adaptation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when the number of labeled samples per class in the target domain is small, the use of second-and higher-order statistics can help to achieve a more reliable adaptation of the source knowledge.
, when the target domain is only slightly different from the source one, the mixture of alignments can help in the transfer.

, in the context of domain adaptation, second- or even higher-order statistics are more informative than the commonly used first-order (mean) statistics, and that the proposed So-HoT approach is a viable option for the supervised target scenario.
